messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur is a 66-year-old software engineer who has been married for thirty-five years. He presented for therapy at the urging of his wife, Maria, who described him as having become a “ghost in his own house” over the past year. For most of his adult life, Arthur managed to contain the memories of his childhood. He rarely spoke of the years spent in his uncle’s care, a period punctuated by unpredictable and violent punishments. One memory, however, remained particularly vivid: being locked in the cellar for hours, the damp, cold concrete floor pressed against his cheek, his small heart hammering against his ribs as he waited for the heavy footsteps to return. He learned early that the world was a place where you had to be especially careful, because you never knew what could happen next.

For decades, the structured logic of programming provided a refuge. In the clean, predictable world of code, there were no sudden threats. He built a quiet life with Maria, who understood his need for space and his aversion to large social gatherings. The past was a locked room he rarely entered. That changed at his retirement party last spring. A younger colleague, wishing him well, clapped him firmly on the back. The sudden, unexpected touch sent a jolt through Arthur’s body. Before he could even process the man’s friendly intention, his body had already reacted as if to a blow; his heart began to pound violently in his chest, and for a split second, he felt the chilling cold of the cellar floor on his skin. This sudden cascade of physical sensation and intrusive memory immediately activated a profound sense of threat, confirming his deeply held belief that people simply cannot be trusted and that safety is an illusion.

In the months that followed, this belief that he was fundamentally unsafe and that others were untrustworthy began to dictate his entire existence. To manage the overwhelming feeling of danger, Arthur began to systematically dismantle his life. He stopped attending the weekly breakfast club with other retired engineers, certain that any one of them could pose an unknowable risk. This avoidance of social contact was not just about others; he started avoiding his own reflection, refusing to look at his own body in the mirror, as if it too were a potential source of betrayal. Most painfully for Maria, he began to avoid any form of physical contact. A hand on his arm or a simple hug would cause him to flinch and pull away, leaving a chasm of silence between them. He had come to believe this was the only way to stay safe.

This new life of constant vigilance has only amplified his sense of ambient threat. His conviction that he must always be on guard means he is perpetually scanning his environment for danger. When sitting in his own living room, his eyes are drawn not to the family photos but to the heavy brass lamp on the end table, which his mind instantly catalogues as a potential weapon. This heightened state of alert makes him exquisitely sensitive to the very triggers he is trying to avoid. Because he is always listening for danger, he is constantly aware of his own heartbeat, and the slightest increase in its rhythm can send a fresh wave of panic through him, bringing with it the memory of the cellar. The avoidance itself has become a trap; by isolating himself in his study for hours on end, the silence and lack of external stimuli only make it more likely that an intrusive memory will surface, unbidden.

The strategies he uses to protect himself have, in a cruel irony, reinforced his most painful beliefs. Each time he declines an invitation or sidesteps Maria’s touch, the momentary feeling of relief is quickly replaced by a profound sense of alienation. The isolation proves what he has long suspected: he is permanently an outsider, fundamentally different from everyone else. This withdrawal has also intensified his hypervigilance. Confined to his home, his world has shrunk, and every small stimulus within it feels magnified. The simple act of his wife touching his shoulder as he works at his desk now provokes an alarmed physical startle, a reaction that happens so fast it feels entirely outside his control. He came to therapy after Maria found him sitting alone in the dark, having refused to join her for dinner. He told her he just wanted to be left alone, but what he admitted in session was his deepest fear: that by trying so desperately to protect himself, he was ensuring he would end up completely, terrifyingly alone.
